title: Human Laboratory Investigation of Tobacco Withdrawal and Smoking Relapse in Smokers with and without Major Depression
abstract: Smokers with major depressive disorder (MDD) are more susceptible to tobacco dependence and experience more difficulty quitting than those without MDD. Within this high tobacco burden population, the process of tobacco withdrawal and implications for smoking relapse have been reported in epidemiologic studies, but there has been little experimental research. This study sought to investigate affective and cognitive symptoms of tobacco withdrawal in MDD. Data were analyzed from a laboratory study that manipulated withdrawal in adult smokers with and without MDD. Participants abstained from smoking for 48 hours (confirmed using breath carbon monoxide ≤10 ppm) and completed questionnaires assessing affective and cognitive withdrawal symptoms at baseline while smoking as usual and again after 48 hours of abstinence. Participants were re-contacted at 1 month to assess their abstinence status. Participants included 32 smokers, 19 with MDD (MDD+) and 13 without MDD (MDD-), with a mean age of 37.5 (SD=12.0). Compared with MDD- smokers, MDD+ smokers showed significantly greater changes in both affective and cognitive dimensions of withdrawal. By one month, 84.6% of MDD+ smokers relapsed compared to 52.6% of MDD- smokers. This study is the first to distinguish and compare affective and cognitive symptom response to acute abstinence among smokers with MDD and explore the implications for relapse. Although preliminary, greater relapse for MDD smokers may be due to greater overall severity of withdrawal as opposed to greater severity in depression-related withdrawal symptoms. Further experimental research is needed to better understand how acute withdrawal may undermine quitting for MDD smokers.
